sources.news_title: Ocasio-Cortez Says She'll Freeze Her Eggs
sources.text:
"Usually I keep my private life quite private," Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez said in a series of videos newly posted to social media before announcing an exception. "I have made the decision to start freezing my eggs," she said. The New York congresswoman acknowledging there's a "political risk" in talking about the matter but saying that won't drive her choices, the New York Times reports. Ocasio-Cortez said she's going public to normalize "women having full lives in every context and every choice," and called her ability to pursue the procedure a "very privileged position" made feasible by advancing technology.
                                    
                                    
                                
                                
                             
                            
                            
                            
                            
                            
                                
                                
                                    
                                        Egg freezing involves daily hormone injections, frequent monitoring, and a surgical retrieval—costly steps that aren't always covered by insurance. In an interview Sunday on ABC's This Week, Ocasio-Cortez framed her decision as part of a broader conversation about reproductive health, criticizing what she described as an administration limiting access to care, including abortion and healthy pregnancies. On This Week, Ocasio-Cortez also was asked whether she intends to run for president in 2028 or challenge fellow Democrat Chuck Schumer for his Senate seat, per Axios. "Anything is possible at this juncture," she answered.

sources.news_title: Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez Reveals She’s Freezing Her Eggs: ‘I Feel Empowered’
sources.text:
Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez is revealing a new chapter in her private life as she continues to represent New York City’s 14th congressional district.
“Hey everyone, it’s been a minute since I’ve posted to stories, but I think it’s a good time to kind of dive back in again — it’s August recess and I think it’s good for you all to hear a little bit more from me directly,” the congresswoman, 36, said via her Instagram Stories on Saturday, August, 8, adding that she is “having some things happen” in her life that she wants to “share more” with her followers amid her “reflective mood.”
“I want to share with you all a decision that is very personal that I have made that has taken me time to consider, weigh and save up for,” she continued, “And it is of a sensitive matter and a personal matter and usually I keep my private life quite private, but I have made the decision to start freezing my eggs.”
Ocasio-Cortez, who was 29 when she was sworn into Congress after becoming the youngest woman elected to the House of Representatives in 2018, is currently engaged to her longtime partner Riley Roberts. The congresswoman admitted that her decision to freeze her eggs — one she plans to document for her social media followers — was due, in part, to near-constant speculation she will one-day be a frontrunner for the Democratic nominee for president.
“The media will run up and ask a question like, ‘Are you going to run for this? or, ‘Are you going to run for that?’ And it’s almost through this very two-dimensional craven understanding or ambitious understanding of power,” she explained. “When I think a lot of us actually approach these considerations or these decisions through the larger context of our lives as whole human beings and what is happening in our lives as whole human beings.”
Ocasio-Cortez — a common target of President Donald Trump and members of the Republican party — also acknowledged that “strangely” there is a “political risk” or potential “political tax” to her candidly sharing her egg-freezing journey.
“People don’t go down those rabbit holes and fixate on them for men in terms of their decision the way they do for women,” she added. “And I’m not here to, like, talk about what’s fair or unfair in this context — this is just the world that we live in today, and so I’m aware that just by me choosing to not keep this private there may be a consequence.”
She continued, “But you know what, I’m OK with that. This is a choice that I am making to feel more in control of my life and if people want to make assumptions about my decision, let them make those assumptions – I feel empowered to make this choice. I think it’s a very privileged position that I’ve been able to be able to make. And it’s also a result of, I think, changes in technology that have also made it more financially accessible.”
The congresswoman went on to reveal that she took her “first shot this morning” and will have to take multiple injections as part of the egg-freezing process on Sunday, August 9, before her scheduled appearance on an ABC morning show.
“I’m going to be delivering an interview on national television and it’s in the morning and I have to take my shot because of the timing of it,” she said. “I’m gonna be taking my shots in the green room before my interview. And I want you all to see that because women can do anything, and I think it’s badass that I’m gonna be, you know, giving myself shots in the green room, get my glam on, roll out talk about international events, domestic policy, elections, pop out, live my life, do my thing.”
She continued, “If we want community we have to raise our hand and be community for each other, so that’s what we’re going to do.”

sources.news_title: AOC Freezes Her Eggs After Telling Others To Question Having Kids
sources.text:
Socialist Congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-NY) announced Saturday that she is freezing her eggs and filmed herself injecting hormones into her stomach, describing the decision as a “privileged” opportunity to gain more control over how she balances her personal and political life.
“Normally, I keep my private life quite private. But I have made the decision to freeze my eggs. And I want to share this because I was weighing it for a very long time, and there isn’t a ton out there, and it can feel very daunting,” the potential 2028 presidential contender said. “I am aware there is, very strangely, a political ‘risk’ or ‘tax’ that could come with sharing this information.”
In a series of Instagram posts, the 36-year-old, who is childless, described to her millions of followers the “reflective mood” she has been in recently and the pressures that ultimately led to her decision.
“There’s also this flip side where you have to then grow up in the public eye, in a time that most people usually get to grow more privately,” she lamented. “And when you get elected later in life, you’ve made all of your mistakes in private. You’ve learned. You’ve grown in private. But when you get elected in public, and when you’re young, you have to do all of that in public.”
In one video, the self-described Democratic socialist is seen unboxing the medication, lifting her shirt, and injecting herself in the stomach as she begins the egg retrieval process. “Don’t be weird about this, even though I know all of you will be,” she told the camera before administering the shot.
AOC, who was first elected to Congress at age 29, said she is documenting her fertility journey to help educate women about what she described as a lack of awareness surrounding women’s health, including puberty, pregnancy, and menopause.
On the fertility front, it’s a notable shift in tone for the Bronx leftist, who has long championed feminist causes, including abortion-on-demand, while previously telling young people to reconsider having children because of climate change.
“Our planet is going to hit disaster if we don’t turn this ship around, and so it’s basically like, there’s a scientific consensus that the lives of children are going to be very difficult,” Ocasio-Cortez said in a February 2019 Instagram live video. “And it does lead, I think, young people to have a legitimate question, you know, ‘Is it okay to still have children?’”
A woman’s fertility is closely tied to the number and quality of eggs in her ovaries, with age playing a major role in egg quality. Research has found that fertility declines significantly with age, with women in their mid-30s generally having lower chances of conceiving than women in their 20s, according to Trianglen Fertility Clinic. By the late 30s, fertility declines further, and after 41 years, the egg quality declines rapidly.
For AOC, the biological clock is ticking — and she knows it.
“I feel empowered to make this choice. I think it’s a very privileged position that I’ve been able to make, and it’s also a result of, I think, changes in technology that have also made it more financially accessible,” she said. “This is a choice that I am making to feel more in control of my life.”

Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez is freezing her eggs, and, if you’d like to follow along, she’s filming and sharing the journey online. “I think we need to have more depictions of women living full lives in every context and every choice,” she said.
On Saturday, the congresswoman posted a series of Instagram stories announcing that she’d made the “very personal” decision to freeze her eggs. She concluded with a short vlog of herself preparing her medications and administering her very first shot. “Don’t be weird about this,” she told the camera. “Even though I know all of you will be.”
On Sunday, AOC spoke candidly about freezing her eggs on ABC This Morning. She noted that it’s important to share and normalize these processes, “in this political environment where this administration is denying reproductive care to women across the country, from abortion rights to the ability to carry out a healthy pregnancy.”
This isn’t actually the first time AOC has talked about her own fertility publicly. In 2020, she discussed the possibility of freezing her eggs in an interview with Vanity Fair. “It’s important for us to talk about it, because women, we have to make these choices that men simply don’t have to make,” she said.

The congresswoman said Congress’ August recess gave her the time and space to begin the process, adding that she felt “empowered” by the decision.
“This is a choice that I am making to feel more in control of my life,” said the prominent New York Democrat, who represents parts of the Bronx and Queens. “And if people want to make assumptions about my decision, let them make those assumptions. I feel empowered to make this choice.”
Ocasio-Cortez also appeared to address ongoing speculation about her political future, including chatter about a possible 2028 presidential run, while arguing that elected officials weigh major life choices for reasons that go beyond political ambition.
“The media will run up and ask a question like, ‘Are you going to run for this? Or are you going to run for that?’ And it is almost through this very two-dimensional, craven understanding or ambitious understanding of power,” she said.

“I want you all to see that. And because women can do anything, and I think it’s badass that I’m going to be giving myself shots in the green room [as I] get my glam on,” she said.
Egg-harvesting allows women to have some of their unfertilized eggs taken from their ovaries when younger and then store them at subzero temperatures till they are ready to have them implanted either in themselves or a surrogate.
The process increases their chances of a successful pregnancy later in life, as women’s egg quality often declines rapidly in their mid-30s.
To freeze their eggs, women have to go through about two weeks of hormone treatment before undergoing the procedure to harvest their eggs.
“This is just not something that men deal with,” AOC said.
“Men run for office, or frankly, they interview for jobs, and people don’t think in the back of their mind, ‘Okay, this guy is running for office. How old is he? Oh, well, is he going to want to start a family,’ ” she said.

“I got sworn into the House of Representatives when I was 29 years old,” she reflected. “There’s this flip side where you have to then grow up in the public eye in a time that most people usually get to grow more privately.”

Firebrand progressive AOC gets intimately personal about her health on Instagram live: ‘This is a choice’
Speaking to her followers, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez criticized the systemic lack of education surrounding women’s bodies
New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez revealed to her followers — and the world — that she was freezing her eggs, sharing a live video on her Instagram story during which she administered a hormone injection to herself ahead of a scheduled Sunday television appearance.
“Usually, I keep my private life quite private, but I have made the decision to start freezing my eggs,” Ocasio-Cortez said in the Saturday night live stream, “and I want to share that with anyone who is — and I want to share this because I was weighing it for a very long time, and I think that, you know, I was saving for it for a very long time, and there just isn’t a ton out there, I feel, and sometimes it can feel very daunting.”
The Democratic congresswoman discussed the preparation involved in the medical procedure and noted that taking her first injection “wasn’t so bad.” She mentioned that she would be administering additional doses in the green room before appearing on ABC’s This Week.
“As women in general, we are not taught about our bodies, we are not prepared for our own lives, whether that is in puberty, whether that is in pregnancy, whether that is in perimenopause, menopause, whether that is in so many different aspects of our lives,” she said.
Reflecting on her public profile and reproductive choices, Ocasio-Cortez explained her rationale for sharing the experience publicly despite the personal nature of the procedure.
“In the political context that we're in, in an administration that is dedicated to politicizing women’s bodies and taking our choices away from us and punishing us around decisions to be pregnant or not be pregnant — and, frankly, this administration has made pregnancy more dangerous than probably at any point in the last 30 plus years — we’re gonna take our power back,” she said.
She noted that navigating adulthood while serving in Congress presented unique challenges, particularly regarding reproductive decisions and public scrutiny.
“I got sworn into the House of Representatives when I was 29 years old. I was the youngest woman in American history to get elected to congress,” Ocasio-Cortez said. “There’s also this flip side where you have to then grow up in the public eye in a time that most people usually get to grow more privately, and when you get elected later in life you've made all of your mistakes in private.”
She also highlighted double standards faced by female politicians regarding family planning and age.
“This is just not something that men deal with. Men run for office, or frankly, they interview for jobs and people don't think in the back of their mind, ‘OK this guy's running for office, how old is he? Oh, well is he gonna wanna start a family?’” she said. “This is a choice I am making to feel more in control of my life.”
She acknowledged potential fallout, too.
“I am also aware that there is very strangely a political risk, or even a political tax that could come with sharing this information, and, per usual, that doesn't influence my ultimate decision,” she said.
Ocasio-Cortez has frequently advocated for reproductive healthcare. Following the U.S. Supreme Court's decision to overturn Roe v. Wade, she told GQ in a 2022 interview that men also had a stake in reproductive freedom.
“For almost every woman that has gotten an abortion, there’s a man who has either been affected or liberated by that abortion too,” she told the publication at the time.
Her decision to document the fertility treatment drew immediate responses on social media.
Democratic strategist Xochitl Hinojosa praised the disclosure on X, writing: “THIS. We don’t talk about women freezing their eggs or what women have to go through to start a family. Thank you @AOC for your bravery.”
Other commentators reacted critically to the video and its framing.
User @thewakeninq wrote on X: “AOC just injected herself on camera, told everyone ‘don’t be weird,’ then acted shocked when the internet lost its mind. It’s not diabetes. It’s not a baby. It’s her freezing eggs so she can maybe have one later… while spending her entire career fighting to make sure other women can end theirs. The cognitive dissonance is Olympic-level. Don’t be weird? Too late.”

sources.text:
'Empowered' AOC films egg freezing journey and opens up on sad 'political risk'
AOC revealed that she recently froze her eggs and wanted to "share with you all a decision that is very personal that I've made that has taken me time to consider, weigh and save up for," she said in the video
New York Rep. Alexandra Ocasio-Cortez has opened up about starting her egg freezing journey on Instagram, saying she was "empowered" amid a tough political landscape for women.
Popular Democrat AOC revealed that she recently decided to freeze her eggs and wanted to "share with you all a decision that is very personal that I've made that has taken me time to consider, weigh and save up for," she said in the video. It comes as conservatism has swept over reproductive rights in recent years with the overturn of Roe. V. Wade in 2022 and, more recently, the temporary ban of abortion pills. The latter was temporarily restored by the Supreme Court in May.
The US congressman explained: "Normally, I keep my private life quite private. But I have made the decision to freeze my eggs. And I want to share this because I was weighing it for a very long time, and there isn't a ton out there, and it can feel very daunting."
In a candid video, Ocasio-Cortez recorded herself unboxing the medications she will use during the process before preparing to take her first injection.
Then, just before the needle went in, she delivered a characteristically blunt warning to her audience. “Don’t be weird about this even though I know you all will be,” she joked.
The light-hearted moment came as she addressed a much more serious issue: what women are — and are not — taught about their own bodies.
Ocasio-Cortez said women are often not given enough information about subjects including puberty, fertility and menopause. By sharing her own experience, she hopes to offer a more realistic depiction of women's lives and make a potentially intimidating process easier for others to understand.
But she knows that putting such personal information into the public arena comes with risks.
The congresswoman acknowledged that there could be a political “risk” or “tax” attached to discussing her fertility and reproductive choices publicly.
She pointed out that women in public life can face questions and assumptions that men generally do not. Men running for office or interviewing for jobs are rarely subjected to speculation about their age and whether they might want to start a family, she argued. Women, meanwhile, can find those questions lurking in the background of public discussion.
By discussing her decision, Ocasio-Cortez knows she may invite exactly that kind of scrutiny. But she appears unwilling to let it dictate her choices.
AOC said: "I am aware there is very strangely a political 'risk' or 'tax' that could come with sharing this information. I'm aware that in all of this swirling conversation that happens that I am now opening the door to this being part of that discussion.
"This is not something men deal with. Men run for office and interview for jobs and people don't think in the back of their mind 'how old is he, is he going to want to start a family?' People don't go down those rabbit holes and fixate on that for men the way they do for women.
“This is a choice I am making to feel more in control of my life. If people want to make assumptions about my decision, let them.”
For Ocasio-Cortez, the decision is ultimately about empowerment and planning for the future on her own terms. She also plans to continue documenting the experience for her followers.
She aid she would take another shot on Sunday morning in the green room at ABC before appearing for an interview, while answering questions from followers throughout the process.

It is an unusually personal look at a woman whose public life is normally dominated by politics.
But this time, Ocasio-Cortez wants the conversation to be about something much more universal: women, their bodies, their choices — and the freedom to make deeply personal decisions without having them defined by anyone else.
